title: A Rustle in the Loft
story:
The storm spent the remainder of the night hammering against the sagging cedar shingles of the old barn, but by dawn, the deluge had softened to a hollow, steady drip from the rafters. James awoke curled tight in a fragrant mound of old hay, his brass canister tucked safely against his chest. Through the wide cracks in the timber siding, pale daylight filtered into the dusty gloom in slanted bars of grey and gold, revealing the barn's neglected skeletal bones—broken cart wheels, rusted scythe blades, and long-abandoned grain bins.

He listened closely before moving, letting the quiet settle in his ears. He listened for the angry shouts of the villagers who had slammed their shutters yesterday. He listened for the howling gale that had chased him down from the ridge. But there was neither shout nor wind—only the slow, rhythmic drop of collected rainwater striking an upturned tin bucket in the center of the earthen floor.

Then came a sound that had nothing to do with rain: a scratch, a rapid scurry, and the dry rattle of a cracked acorn shell rolling across a floorboard overhead. James tilted his head back. Peering over the splintered edge of the hayloft was not an owl or a barn swallow, but a small highland deer mouse with oversized, translucent ears and whiskers that twitched with manic, electric energy. The creature did not freeze or flee upon seeing James. Instead, he cocked his head, leaned out precariously far over the drop, and let out an inquisitive, indignant squeak, as if demanding to know who had authorized an overnight guest in his private citadel.

James sat up slowly, moving with the measured care he had practiced in Don Tadeo's workshop, keeping his palms open and low. Reaching into the fold of his leather strap, he carefully retrieved the dried star-shaped seed pod he had carried all the way from the Grand Library's folios. He did not toss it. He merely placed it gently on an exposed timber beam between them, stepped back, and bowed his head slightly in respectful greeting.

The little mouse scrambled down the post in a brazen, zigzagging dash, wholly devoid of hesitation. He circled the pod twice, gave it a series of vigorous sniffing nudges, and looked straight up into James's eyes with a tilt of utter curiosity. In a town where every door had been barred against him, this tiny, fearless watchman seemed more than willing to inspect the stranger on his own terms.
